61.title: 7 SEO Tips That Actually Grow Your Small Business's Organic Traffic
61.description: Concrete, practical SEO steps for small businesses — not in theory, but in the order they actually deliver results.
61.keywords: SEO tips, small business SEO, grow organic traffic, SEO for beginners, local SEO
texts: [davelopment]®

sees it every day: most small business owners have heard of SEO but have no idea where to start — or they start in the wrong place, spending on logo animations and colour schemes before the most basic technical things are in order. These 7 steps follow the order that actually matters.
1. Technical basics first, content second

Writing articles for a slow site that works poorly on mobile is wasted effort — both Google and visitors turn away before they read anything. Check how long your site takes to load and whether it is genuinely comfortable to use on a phone. If your website itself is slow,
we wrote about it in more detail here
2. Focus on one specific, local keyword — not everything at once

As a small business you can't compete with a national brand for a generic term. A location-bound, specific phrase is a far more realistic target — e.g. "accountant in Debrecen" instead of "accounting". There is much less competition for these, and the visitor gets exactly what they were looking for.
3. Google Business Profile — if you want local customers, it isn't optional
A fully completed, up-to-date Google Business Profile (opening hours, photos, genuine reviews) often brings more than a month of article writing — especially for local, service-based businesses.
4. Regular, fresh content — not a one-off sprint

Google (and now AI-powered search tools such as ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews) rewards sites that are updated regularly. One or two genuinely useful articles a month beat a month-long sprint you forget about afterwards.
5. Structured, easy-to-read content
Short paragraphs, clear subheadings, concrete answers at the top — this is good not only for the reader but also for how AI search tools extract and quote your content.
6. Measure, don't guess
Without Google Search Console you don't even know which keywords you appear for — you're working blind. Set it up and review it at least once a month.
7. If you don't have the time, don't do it halfway
Half-configured, neglected SEO is worse than consciously skipping it — it gives you a false sense of security. If you don't have the capacity to work on it regularly, consider choosing

62.title: Which Design Elements Increase a Landing Page's Conversion Rate?
62.description: Concrete, proven design decisions that bring in more submitted forms or orders — not just good looks.
62.keywords: landing page conversion, landing page design, conversion rate optimization, CTA button, form conversion
texts: [davelopment]®

designs every landing page from this angle: the goal of a landing page isn't to look beautiful — it's to get the visitor to take the desired action. Every design element has to serve that, otherwise it's just decoration.
One call-to-action button, not ten

If five different buttons compete for attention on your page ("Request a quote", "Read more", "Subscribe", "Call us"...), the visitor won't press any of them — the decision load is too high. Have one main action; anything else should be a secondary, more understated option at most.
The first screen (without scrolling) should answer "what do I get?"
Most visitors don't scroll down — if it isn't clear within the first second what you offer and to whom, they leave. The headline shouldn't be a slogan but a concrete promise.
Social proof — but real

A specific review with a name or company attached is worth far more than a generic "our clients are satisfied" line. If you have genuine references, show them — fictional or exaggerated claims achieve exactly the opposite.
A short form with fewer fields
Every extra field you ask for lowers the completion rate. Ask yourself for each field: do you really need it right now, or can it wait until a phone call?
It has to work just as well on mobile
Most traffic now comes from mobile — if the button is hard to reach on a phone or the form is awkward to fill in, most of your conversions are lost right there, before anything else could go wrong.
Don't make the design the star
An over-designed page crammed with animations distracts from what matters. Good conversion design is often invisible — the visitor doesn't notice the layout, they focus on what you're telling them.

63.title: How to Actually Generate Leads With Your Website (Not Just Visitors)
63.description: Traffic on its own isn't revenue — this is the difference between a website that simply "exists" and one that actually brings in customers.
63.keywords: lead generation website, website lead generation, getting customers online, website conversion, B2B leads
texts: [davelopment]®

meets many business owners in the same situation: they have visitors on their website, yet no enquiries come in. Most of the time the problem isn't the amount of traffic — it's that the site doesn't guide the visitor towards getting in touch.
Make the next step obvious
On every page, ask yourself: if someone gets this far, what exactly should they do now? If the answer isn't clear to you, it will be even less clear to the visitor.
Don't keep your contact details only on a "Contact" page
If the option to get in touch sits on a single, tucked-away subpage, you lose the people who were about to decide on your service page but don't want to click through to yet another page.
Reduce the sense of risk
"Free consultation", "No commitment", "We reply within 24 hours" — these lines aren't decoration; they genuinely reduce the uncertainty that stops someone from submitting the form.
Follow up on what happens after submission
If someone fills in the form and doesn't hear from you for days, that's the experience they take away. A fast, human reply brings conversions (and repeat referrals) on its own.
Measure where your actual enquiries come from
Without this you spend blindly on ads or content for channels that don't actually deliver — while underfunding a channel that performs well.

64.title: I'm Starting a Business — Should I Build the Brand Identity or the Website First?
64.description: The most common question when starting out — and why the answer isn't necessarily the one you'd expect.
64.keywords: brand identity or website first, startup branding, brand identity design, website for a new business, logo design
texts: [davelopment]®
hears this question more than almost any other from people who are just starting a business — the answer isn't black and white, but there's one practical consideration that often settles it.
You don't need a finished brand identity first

Many people put off their website because they think they first need a "finished" brand identity (logo, colours, typeface). In reality, a well-structured website design process includes shaping the visual direction too — there's no need to treat them as two separate projects.
The website is what actually makes money

A logo on its own doesn't generate revenue. A website that can be found and is convincing does. If your budget or time is tight, what brings in customers deserves priority over what is "merely" beautiful.
But an inconsistent brand erodes trust
If your website, your Facebook page and your business cards all look different, it gives an amateur impression — precisely with the decision-makers for whom trust matters most.
The practical answer: both at once, from one team
The best results come when the website and the brand identity are built by one team, each building on the other — not bouncing between two separate contractors on two separate schedules.

65.title: How to Keep a Consistent Brand Identity Across Your Website and Social Media
65.description: Practical steps to make your business look and sound the same everywhere — without having to build a design studio for it.
65.metaTitle: Consistent Branding on Web and Social — [davelopment]©
65.keywords: consistent brand identity, brand consistency, social media branding, brand guidelines, brand building
texts: [davelopment]®

sees it often: many small businesses' websites and Instagram pages look as if they belonged to two different companies — different colours, a different tone, a different logo version. This isn't an aesthetic detail; it's a matter of trust.
A fixed, small colour palette
You don't need 10 colours — 2–3 main colours and 1–2 accents are enough, used consistently everywhere: on your website, your posts and your story templates.
The same tone of voice everywhere

If your website is formal and your social media posts are casual, visitors can't tell which one is the "real" business. Your tone (formal or friendly, serious or humorous) should be a conscious decision, and you should keep it everywhere.
A clean set of logos
Have one main logo version and one or two simplified variants (e.g. icon only, a round version for profile pictures) — don't redesign it separately for every platform.
Make the website the "hub" everything points to

Social media is great for day-to-day presence, but the final, detailed, reliable information (prices, services, contact details) should always live on your website — direct people there from everywhere.

66.title: What to Watch Out for When Building a B2B Website With SEO Optimization
66.description: B2B websites work differently from B2C sites — the decision process is different, different keywords are worth targeting, and different content persuades.
66.metaTitle: B2B Website SEO: What to Watch Out For — [davelopment]©
66.keywords: B2B website, B2B SEO, B2B website development, B2B keywords, B2B content marketing
texts: [davelopment]®

knows this well: B2B purchasing decisions take longer, pass through more people and are rarely made in a single visit. This fundamentally shapes how a B2B website and its SEO strategy should be built.
Keywords are more specific, volumes are smaller
Far fewer people typically search for a B2B service than for a consumer product — but those who do are much closer to a decision. What matters here isn't the quantity of traffic but its quality.
Content should prove, not just promise
A B2B decision-maker doesn't buy on a slogan — they look for concrete case studies, numbers and references. The more specific and verifiable your claims, the more credible you are.
More decision-makers = more types of content

B2B decisions often involve several people (e.g. the day-to-day user and the manager responsible for the budget) — it's worth including content aimed at both, rather than writing from a single perspective.
Technical SEO is a baseline requirement here too

B2B decision-makers also start their search on Google — or, increasingly, in AI assistants. If your site is technically slow or poorly structured, you're out of the race before you can introduce yourself.
